title: Rigid Band Shift in Electron-Doped Kagome Metal
authors: M. Pinterić, E. Uykur, S. Salters, G. Pokharel, S. D. Wilson, M. Dressel, M. Wenzel
abstract: We study the effects of Sn-site doping on the electronic structure of nonmagnetic kagome metal YV$_6$Sn$_{6-x}$Sb$_x$ by infrared spectroscopy and density-functional theory. The results for samples with $x$ = 0 and 1.4 demonstrate that partial substitution of Sn by Sb acts as a rigid shift of the Fermi level while leaving the band dispersion largely intact. Our findings establish Sn-site substitution in YV$_6$Sn$_6$ as a route to systematically investigate band-filling-dependent electronic properties of nonmagnetic kagome metals.
summary: This work examines how substituting Sn with Sb in the kagome metal YV6Sn6 tunes its electronic properties by shifting the Fermi level. Using a combination of infrared spectroscopy and DFT, the authors demonstrate that this doping preserves the band dispersion while allowing access to different electronic regimes. This provides a powerful route to study band-filling effects in correlated materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how Sn-site doping with Sb affects the electronic structure and optical properties of the nonmagnetic kagome metal YV6Sn6.
main_result: Sb substitution acts as a rigid shift of the Fermi level, allowing systematic tuning of band-filling-dependent electronic properties while preserving the underlying band dispersion.
method: The research combines experimental measurements (infrared spectroscopy, DC resistivity) with theoretical calculations using Density-Functional Theory (DFT) and the Drude-Lorentz model.
model_or_system: The physical system is the kagome metal YV6Sn6, which is doped by substituting Sn with Sb (YV6Sn(6-x)Sb_x). The analysis focuses on the electronic response to changes in electron count.
key_observables: Temperature-dependent resistivity, optical conductivity ($\sigma(\omega, T)$), plasma edge ($\omega_{	ext{screened}}^p$), and interband optical transitions.
important_parameters: Doping concentration ($x$), temperature ($T$), and the Fermi level position relative to specific band features (e.g., Van Hove singularities).
main_assumptions: The doping effect is modeled primarily as a rigid shift of the Fermi level, suggesting the underlying band structure remains largely intact.
figures_summary: Figures compare temperature-dependent resistivity and optical spectra between pristine and doped samples, showing shifts in plasma edges and changes in spectral weight across different energy ranges.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first characterizing the doping effect via transport and optical measurements, then using DFT to model the band structure evolution, and finally mapping the changes in interband transitions as the Fermi level is systematically shifted by doping.
why_interesting: The ability to tune the Fermi level systematically via chemical doping in a correlated material like a kagome metal provides a clean experimental handle to map out the electronic structure dependence on filling, which is crucial for understanding correlated electron physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Four-probe dc resistivity of YV6Sn6 (a) and YV6Sn4.6Sb1.4 (b) measured on the samples used in the opti- cal experiments. Black squares represent the resistivity values obtained from the Hagen-Rubens fits to the low-energy reflec- tivities.

FIG. 3. Comparison of the optical spectra of pristine YV6Sn6 and YV6Sn4.6Sb1.4 at T = 10 K. The measured reflectivity is plotted in panel (a). The inset shows the zero crossing of the real part of the dielectric permittivity, marking the screened plasma frequency ωscreened p = ωp/√ε∞. Panel (b) presents the calculated real part of the optical conductivity.

FIG. 2. (a)(b) Temperature-dependent reflectivity of YV6Sn6 and YV6Sn4.6Sb1.4, respectively, measured in the ab plane. (c)(d) Corresponding real parts of the optical conductivity. The low-energy values obtained by the Hagen-Rubens extrap- olation are plotted with dotted lines.

FIG. 4. Exemplary decompositions of the optical conduc- tivity of YV6Sn6 at room temperature (a) and 10 K (b). (c)(d) Same but for the doped sample. The spectra are mod- eled by a Drude peak (blue), a localization peak (purple), and multiple Lorentzians describing the interband transitions (dark green). In pristine YV6Sn6, an additional phonon mode is resolved (orange). (e) Temperature evolution of the posi- tion of the localization peak. Error bars of 20 cm−1 are as- sumed. (f) Drude scattering rates obtained from the fits.

FIG. 5. Interband contribution to the optical conductiv- ity. (a) Experimental interband optical conductivity obtained by subtracting the modeled intraband contributions (Drude + localization peaks) and the phonon mode from the data. Characteristic modifications observed in the doped sample are highlighted by blue and green arrows. (b)(c) DFT-derived in- terband absorption for the stoichiometric case as well as for electron-doped calculations. The experimentally observed in- terband transitions in the doped case are well reproduced by adding 1.4 electrons per formula unit [red curve in panel (c)].
